lead: Memory arrays fail in ways logic does not. A cell can disturb its neighbour, a row can fail to switch, and the address decoder can select no cell, two cells, or the wrong cell. A vector set built for stuck-at faults in random logic misses these. Memories are therefore tested with ordered read/write sequences called march algorithms. The same tests run at wafer sort, final test, and inside the chip through memory BIST.
prereq: You need SRAM and DRAM cell structure and decoders from Unit 4, and stuck-at and coupling ideas from 6.2.

sections.h3: Fault models the tester must excite

blocks.text: A memory is not a bag of independent bits when it is tested. The tester sees five blocks: the address decoder, the cell array, the sense amplifiers, the write drivers, and the read/write control. A defect in any block produces a pattern that a plain stuck-at vector set misses. The cell array is a grid, so a write to one cell can disturb a neighbour. The decoder is a tree of gates, so a bad address can open no row, two rows, or the wrong row.

head: Fault model
Meaning
rows: Aggressor changes victim: inversion flips it, idempotent forces a value; state needs a level, dynamic needs a transition.
No cell accessed, multiple cells accessed, or wrong cell.
Cell value depends on a pattern in nearby cells.
Cell loses data after a pause or without refresh.

blocks.text: Coupling faults always name an aggressor and a victim. A test must write the aggressor, then read the victim, in both orders. Only a few universities teach neighbourhood pattern sensitive fault coverage in detail; the idea is that a cell's value depends on a pattern in its neighbours.

Let n be the number of words in the memory. A march test is a sequence of march elements. Each element has a direction and one or more operations. The symbol ⇑ means ascending address order; ⇓ means descending. w0 writes 0. r1 reads and expects 1; a mismatch is a fail. r0 reads and expects 0.

blocks.where: L is total memory accesses; k is operations per cell summed over all march elements; n is number of words.

head: Test
Length
rows: about 2n² for one pattern, more for both

blocks.text: March tests are linear because each element visits every cell once or a few times. Walking and GALPAT are quadratic: for each base cell they write or read all other cells. A 1 Mb array at 4n² is too slow for production, so O(n²) tests are used on small arrays or for diagnosis. March C− covers stuck-at, transition, coupling, and address decoder faults in 10n accesses.

sections.h3: Memory BIST and the logic around the array

blocks.text: Memory BIST puts the test engine on chip. The controller has five parts: an algorithm sequencer that stores the march elements, an address counter that counts up or down, a data generator for writes and expected reads, a comparator, and a multiplexer that switches the array from functional logic to BIST mode.

items: Sequencer selects the next march element and its direction.
Data generator drives w0 or w1 and supplies expected data.
Comparator checks each read and sets pass or fail.
Multiplexer returns the array to functional mode.

blocks.text: The logic around the array needs its own vectors. Address wrap logic, data wrap logic, byte enables, and ECC can hide a cell fault. BIST must test through that logic or mux it out. Algorithmic optimisation chooses a march variant that covers the same fault list with fewer operations; MATS+ is 5n but weaker, March C− is 10n and stronger.

figure.caption: March tests cost 10n accesses; GALPAT costs about 4n², so it is used only on tiny arrays.

spec.aria: Plot showing memory accesses growing linearly for a march test and quadratically for GALPAT, the gap widening as the number of cells increases.

examples.question: A 1024-word embedded SRAM is tested with March C−. March C− has six elements: M0 ⇑w0, M1 ⇑r0w1, M2 ⇓r1w0, M3 ⇑r0w1, M4 ⇓r1w0, M5 ⇑r0. Count the operations per cell and the total accesses. At 5 ns per access, find the test time. Compare with GALPAT, which needs about 4n² accesses.
steps: Count operations per cell: M0=1, M1=2, M2=2, M3=2, M4=2, M5=1. Sum = 10.
examples.answer: March C− needs 10,240 accesses and 51.2 µs; GALPAT needs 4,194,304 accesses and 20.97152 ms, about 409.6 times longer, so the march test is the production choice.
examples.check:
n = 1024
ops = 10
accesses = ops * n
t_ns = 5
time_us = accesses * t_ns / 1000
galpat = 4 * n * n
galpat_ms = galpat * t_ns / 1000000
ratio = galpat / accesses
print(accesses)
print(time_us)
print(galpat)
print(galpat_ms)
print(ratio)

traps: Treating a memory as a set of independent stuck-at cells. Without ordered writes and reads in both directions, transition and coupling faults are never excited, and address decoder faults need the ascending and descending passes.
Confusing 10n with 10n². March C− is linear in n. Only walking and GALPAT are quadratic.
Forgetting that r1 means read and expect 1, not write 1. w and r are different operations.
Assuming BIST tests the array alone. Address wrap logic, data wrap logic, byte enables, and ECC must be included or muxed out.

quiz.q: In a march test, what does n denote?
quiz.a: n is the number of words or cells in the memory array.

quiz.q: Why can a stuck-at vector set miss a coupling fault?
quiz.a: It does not write the aggressor cell and then read the victim cell in the required order, so the disturbance is never excited and observed.

quiz.q: March C− is run on a 256-word memory. How many memory accesses does the test need?
Why does GALPAT cost about 4n² accesses, and when is it used?
quiz.a: For each base cell it writes or reads all other cells, giving quadratic growth. It is used on small arrays or for diagnosis, not production test of large memories.

quiz.q: What does ⇓ mean in a march element?
quiz.a: Addresses are visited in descending order.

quiz.q: Name the three address decoder faults.
quiz.a: No cell accessed, multiple cells accessed, and wrong cell accessed.

quiz.q: What is the job of the multiplexer in a memory BIST controller?
quiz.a: It switches the memory array from functional logic to BIST mode, and switches it back after test.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production memories add ECC and repair: a BIST pass can fuse in spare rows or columns. Automotive and medical chips run memory BIST at every power-up because latent faults matter. 3D stacked DRAM and in-memory computing make coupling and thermal patterns harder to model. Search next for memory BIST, March SS, and row-hammer testing.
